## bioRxiv
An MCP server for accessing bioRxiv and medRxiv preprint servers.

This server provides:
- Tools: Search preprints, get preprint details, list subject categories
- Prompts: Analyze preprint methodology and findings

bioRxiv is a preprint server for biological sciences operated by Cold Spring
Harbor Laboratory. It hosts research manuscripts that have NOT undergone peer
review. This server wraps the official bioRxiv API to provide structured access
to preprint metadata, abstracts, and full-text PDFs.

TOOL SELECTION GUIDE:
• search_preprints: Find preprints by date range and/or subject category (no keyword, author, or full-text search) - primary discovery tool
• get_preprint: Get full details for a specific preprint by DOI
• get_categories: List available subject categories for filtering
• search_published_preprints: Find preprints that have been formally published in journals
• funder_search: Find preprints by funding source (NIH, etc.)
• get_statistics: Usage and submission statistics

MULTI-TOOL WORKFLOWS:
For comprehensive literature analysis:
1. Use search_preprints to find relevant preprints by date range and category
2. Use get_preprint for detailed information on promising results
3. Use search_published_preprints to check if preprints have been peer-reviewed and published
4. Use funder_search to identify research funding patterns in a field

For tracking research trends:
1. Use get_categories to identify relevant subject areas
2. Use search_preprints with date filters for recent activity
3. Use get_statistics to understand submission volumes

## Claude_Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## Consensus
Consensus is a research paper search engine: relevance-ranked semantic search over 400M+ peer-reviewed papers (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, PubMed). Use the `search` tool to look up papers for a scientific query; it takes plain-language queries and returns ranked paper records. When presenting search results, you MUST cite papers inline using their numbered references from the tool result (e.g. [1], [2], [3]). When discussing findings, always attribute them to specific papers: 'Caffeine improves endurance performance [1] and reduces perceived exertion [3].' At the end of your response, list all cited papers as numbered references with their titles hyperlinked to the URLs from the tool result: [1] [Paper Title](url) (Authors, Year, Journal, Citations). Use the exact paper URLs from the tool result — do not modify, shorten, or regenerate them. Do not omit paper links or summarize results without citing specific papers. IMPORTANT: Some search results end with a sign-up, upgrade, or usage message. When a result has one, you MUST include it at the END of your response word-for-word: do not omit, shorten, or rephrase it. When a result has none, do not add one: never write your own upgrade prompt, search count, or Consensus link. Batch at most 3 search calls at a time to avoid rate limits. For a broad request (a review, screening, finding everything on a topic), make one search with a large page_size rather than many narrower searches. If you receive a rate limit error, wait 30 seconds before retrying. Do NOT apply search filters (year_min, year_max, study_types, domain, human, sample_size_min, sjr_max, controlled, sjr_min, citation_min, open_access, country) unless the user explicitly requests them or clearly expresses intent to narrow results. If the user asks a research question without mentioning filtering criteria, call search with only the query parameter.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

## Google_Drive
This is an MCP server provided by Drive API. The server provides tools for developers to build LLM applications on top of Drive.

## Convention 2026-11-12 — how a delegated resolution's standing is recorded, and when it opens a task's gate

Recorded by an Opus-class model in the same delegated pass, after the independent review of condition (d) (`workplan/2026-11-12-bidirectional-pipeline/DELEGATED-RESOLUTIONS-REVIEW.md`) found that every task gate read only the literal `OD-NN:` and so opened on a delegated line before its check was recorded. **This is a convention for reading the ledger, not an owner ruling**; it changes no ruling and no doctrine, and the owner may replace it.

**Two kinds of line, latest wins.** For each decision of the register `workplan/2026-11-12-bidirectional-pipeline/REMEDIATION-WORKPLAN.md` §8, the ledger carries:
- a status line, `OD-NN STATUS: <value>`, one of: `ANSWERED BY THE OWNER` (written by the session that records the owner's quoted answer), `RESOLVED UNDER DELEGATION`, `WITHDRAWN, REFERRED BACK TO THE OWNER`, `REFERRED BACK TO THE OWNER`;
- for a delegated resolution, a check line, `OD-NN CHECK: <value>`, one of: `not required`, `pending`, `confirmed`, `confirmed with corrections applied`, `referred back`.

Each is read as the last line of its kind for that id: `grep -F "OD-NN STATUS:" references/project-standards.md | tail -1`, and the same for `CHECK:`. A later line supersedes an earlier one; no line is edited.

**The gate.** A task's precondition on a decision is OPEN only when (1) the last status line is `ANSWERED BY THE OWNER`, or (2) the last status line is `RESOLVED UNDER DELEGATION` **and** the last check line is `not required`, `confirmed` or `confirmed with corrections applied`. Every other state is CLOSED, including no status line at all, `pending`, a withdrawn resolution and a referral. **A task whose text requires the owner's own words** (for example the mobility split, T-102) **is open only on `ANSWERED BY THE OWNER`**; a delegated resolution never satisfies it. The one command a task file uses:

```
gate(){ s=$(grep -F "$1 STATUS:" references/project-standards.md | tail -1); c=$(grep -F "$1 CHECK:" references/project-standards.md | tail -1); case "$s" in *"ANSWERED BY THE OWNER"*) echo "$1 OPEN (owner)";; *"RESOLVED UNDER DELEGATION"*) case "$c" in *"not required"*|*confirmed*) echo "$1 OPEN (delegated; ${c#*CHECK: })";; *) echo "$1 CLOSED (check: ${c:-none})";; esac;; *) echo "$1 CLOSED (${s:-no status line})";; esac; }
```

**What it replaces.** The `grep -n -F "OD-NN:"` checks in the task files, which a delegated line, a withdrawn line and an owner's answer all satisfied alike. The `OD-NN:` answer lines stay as the record of what was answered; they no longer open a gate by themselves.

CONDITION: any task or session deciding whether a register decision is settled enough to act on.
ACTION: (1) Run the gate above for each decision the task names; act only on OPEN. (2) For a task that requires the owner's words, act only on `ANSWERED BY THE OWNER`. (3) When recording an owner's answer to a register decision, add the line `OD-NN STATUS: ANSWERED BY THE OWNER` in the same entry. (4) Never edit a status or check line; append a new one.

# Four things to see, and seven questions only you can answer, in plain words

_Written 2026-11-13 by an Opus-class assistant, and corrected the same day after an independent check. On 2026-11-13 you asked whether these decisions could be settled from your earlier rulings, the mission and the project's goal, and you said you don't know the machinery or the code. Nine of the sixteen open questions were settled that way. They are recorded as the assistant's decisions, not yours, and a second, independent assistant has checked each one: it confirmed all nine, with corrections, and agreed that the seven below are yours. Each of the seven either belongs to you under the project's own rules (who the book is for, what counts as lived-experience evidence, which countries are covered, the book's own vocabulary, the rule against writing records by hand), or turns on what you meant by an earlier answer. Each recommendation below is the assistant's, not a ruling. You can answer in one line._

---

## Four things to see first

The independent check found four things you have not been shown. None needs an answer; each says what you can do.

**1. The book can say the evidence disagrees more often than it can say it agrees.** Your earlier answers say that whenever two kinds of evidence of different strength give different values, the book calls them in disagreement. The settled decision on agreement (OD-43) keeps to the book's written definition: the book says the evidence agrees only when controlled research (studies with measured results) and lived-experience evidence (work made with disabled people) give the same value or range. So two research studies, or a research study and a professional guideline, can be called in disagreement but never in agreement. The settled decision did not create this; it was already there. *What you can do:* leave it as it stands, or say that agreement between any two kinds of evidence also counts, as you did for disagreement (for example "OD-43: agreement between any two kinds counts").

**2. The second document for the reading test (question 1 below).** The option you chose earlier also said to run the test "as written" in the plan, and the plan picks its research study by searching the whole collection, not only batch 23 (a set of documents gathered earlier). So option A in question 1 is what that part of your answer already says. The study it finds is from 2015, not from late October: late October is when it was added to the collection. *What you can do:* answer question 1.

**3. Recording "new or existing building" may leave many values without a headline figure.** A settled decision (OD-49) records the type of building, whether the work is new or existing, and indoor or outdoor on each figure, and shows them as separate cases of one value. You ruled earlier that when every figure of a value carries such a condition, the value has no single headline figure and only its cases are shown. Building codes state most of their figures for new work or for existing work, so many values that rest on codes could lose their headline figure. This will be measured on a copy before any stored figure is re-labelled, and the result will be in the work you review. *What you can do:* leave it until the measurement is shown to you, or say now how a value whose every figure carries a condition should be headed.

**4. Provisions such as hearing loops never get a value.** A settled decision (OD-53) lets a research pass mark things such as a hearing loop or a tactile walking surface as "not a measurement". That follows your rules: the book works out a value only for something measured, such as a length, a height or a contrast. But a provision whose question is whether it is there at all is then never given a value or a mark in the book. The gap falls mainly on people who are Deaf or hard of hearing and on blind people. It comes from the rule about what can be measured, not from the settled decision, and it has not been put to you before. *What you can do:* leave it as it stands (such provisions are discussed but get no value), or say you want provisions that are present or absent covered, and the options will be put to you.

---

## 1. Which second document should two readers test themselves on?

**The situation.** The project plans a test. Two assistants each read the same document separately, and we check whether they write down the same figures. This tells readers of the guidebook how much of each figure comes from the source and how much from whoever read it. You approved using "the material from batch 23", because you were told it held one building code and one controlled research study. It holds no research study. It holds only codes, national guidance documents and grey material (reports and guidance outside peer-reviewed research). Two readers agreeing about a table in a building code proves little, because the numbers are printed plainly. The option you chose also said to run the test "as written" in the plan, and the plan picks the research study by a search of the whole collection, not of batch 23. So option A is what that part of your answer already says.

- **A. Use one of the two research studies with the most findings anywhere in the collection** (a 2015 study of wheelchair users pushing up ramps; the tie between the two is broken by the project's own order), fetched again first because its text is not saved. *What it means:* the test tells us how reliably research findings are read, which is where readers most often disagree. It departs from the words "batch 23's material", and keeps to the "as written" part of your answer.
- **B. Use batch 23's national guidance document with the most figures.** *What it means:* this keeps to the words "batch 23's material" and can start at once. But the test then mostly shows that two readers can copy a table, and says little about the harder case.
- **C. You name the document.**

**Assistant's recommendation (not a ruling): A.** It tests the case that matters for the book's honesty, and it is what the "as written" part of your earlier answer says. You will be asked to start the two reading sessions either way.

**To answer:** "OD-44: A", "OD-44: B" or "OD-44: <the document>".

---

## 2. Seventeen countries in the language list that are not in the book's coverage

**The situation.** The project keeps a list of which languages are spoken in which countries, so it knows where to search. That list names 17 countries that are not in the set you chose for coverage (Argentina, Austria, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cyprus, Ecuador, Ethiopia, Ghana, Guatemala, Morocco, Mexico, Peru, the Philippines, Thailand, Tanzania and Uruguay). They are not in the project's official list of countries either. Nothing about them reaches a reader today. The question is only how they are recorded.

- **A. Record them as known countries, marked out of coverage.** *What it means:* nothing changes for readers. The book still covers only the countries you chose. The project keeps them as places it could expand into later, and its records stay consistent. Once recorded they stay recorded, though they can be marked differently later.
- **B. Remove them from the language list.** *What it means:* the list then matches your coverage exactly, but the project loses its note of possible future countries. The project's rule is that records are retired, not deleted, so this would be an exception you grant.

**Assistant's recommendation (not a ruling): A.** It follows your coverage answer of 12 November and keeps the record of possible future countries.

**To answer:** "OD-46: A" or "OD-46: B".

---

## 3. Who is a figure for, when its sentence names no one?

**The situation.** Many code clauses read like "Corridors should be 1100 mm". They name no group of disabled people, no activity (such as moving around or reaching) and no need. You ruled on 12 November that such a provision is not to be filed as "for everyone", and an earlier ruling of 1 September requires every figure to be tied to at least one group, activity or need. So, today, a figure like this cannot be recorded at all. Your 12 November answer also said that a provision under a general disability heading carries only activity and need links. Option A is how those links would be found when the sentence names no activity.

- **A. Tie it to what the measurement is for.** A corridor width serves moving around, including with a wheelchair or another device. The figure is linked to that activity and marked "from what the measurement is for", never presented as the code's own words. *What it means:* every code figure can be used, and readers see which activities it bears on. The link is the project's reasoning, labelled as such. The project decides, once per measurement, every activity it serves. If it lists too few, a group whose need the measurement also serves (a corridor width also serves people who are blind and use a cane or a guide dog, and people who need to rest) is left out of every code figure for it.
- **B. Tie it to the groups the whole document says it serves** (for the Edmonton checklist: people with low vision and people who use mobility devices). *What it means:* simple, but every item in a document then claims the same groups, including items that do not concern them.
- **C. Do not record the figure until a sentence names someone.** *What it means:* nothing is attributed by inference, but most code figures are lost to the book, including the comparison of codes across countries.
- **D. Keep filing them as "for everyone" until you rule item by item.** *What it means:* this goes against your 12 November answer, and the work to remove "for everyone" cannot finish.

**Assistant's recommendation (not a ruling): A.** It keeps the code figures the book needs, it follows your 12 November answer for provisions under a general heading, and the label stops a reader taking the link for the source's words.

**To answer:** "OD-47: A", "B", "C" or "D".

---

## 4. What does "universal" mean on a published value?

**The situation.** Every published value is labelled with one of three design approaches. Universal means for everyone, at the code floor or above it. Population means for a particular group of disabled people. Person means worked out with one person and their occupational therapist. Two of your earlier decisions point different ways:

- In July you approved a set of changes that included a rule: a value resting only on building codes is labelled "universal".
- On 12 November you chose an answer saying "universal" is where the book states that a provision is for everyone. The question put to you then said that "universal" already meant that, which was not correct: the label was being set by the code rule above.

So today a value for wheelchair users that rests only on codes would be labelled "universal", as if it were for everyone. The July rule's purpose was to stop a value resting only on codes from ever being shown as best practice. Under A that protection is kept by the separate codes-only mark, which already exists.

- **A. "Universal" means for everyone.** A value for a named group is labelled "population" even when it rests only on codes. The fact that it rests only on codes is still shown with the weak-evidence mark (○), which has its own place in the records. *What it means:* the label tells readers whom the value is for. This matches the mission's statement that the strength of the evidence and the design approach are separate questions.
- **B. "Universal" means "rests on codes only", as now.** *What it means:* readers cannot tell from the label whether a value is for everyone, and your 12 November answer needs another way to say "for everyone".
- **C. Keep both, as two separate labels.** *What it means:* the "codes only" fact would then be recorded twice, which the project's rules discourage.

**Assistant's recommendation (not a ruling): A.** It matches your 12 November answer and the mission, and it loses nothing, because the codes-only fact is already recorded and shown.

**To answer:** "OD-48: A", "B" or "C".

---

## 5. Does a city accessibility advisory committee's checklist count as lived-experience evidence?

**The situation.** The Edmonton checklist comes from a city's accessibility advisory committee. The book ranks lived-experience evidence from disabled people (co-produced work) as high as controlled research. That ranking rests on disabled people having made the work. The book's definition of lived-experience evidence includes both organisations of disabled people and the outputs of the consultations governments must hold with them under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. A city advisory committee may be the second kind. The checklist does not say who sat on the committee. For now it is treated as grey material, the lower rank.

- **A. Never.** A committee appointed by a city is not an organisation of disabled people, so its documents stay grey. *What it means:* this is safe against overclaiming, but it may undervalue work that disabled members did write, and it reads only the first half of the book's definition.
- **B. Yes, but only when another document we have actually retrieved shows that disabled people wrote it.** Those people are then recorded by name as its co-authors. *What it means:* the higher rank is earned by evidence of who made the work, and the people who made it are credited in the book. Its soundness would still be tested as you ruled for lived-experience evidence; how that test applies to a document that is not a study is one of your open questions.
- **C. You decide each case yourself.** *What it means:* this is the most control, and it adds to your workload.

**Assistant's recommendation (not a ruling): B.** It holds the higher rank to its own reason, that disabled people made the work, and it never removes them from the record.

**To answer:** "OD-51: A", "B" or "C".

---

## 6. Does "barrier-free path of travel" include the route outside the building?

**The situation.** You approved this term and its definition: "a circulation route **through a building** that a person using a wheelchair or other mobility device can travel without barriers". You kept it separate from an "accessible route", which must also work for blind people. The Edmonton checklist uses the same phrase for the outdoor route from the parking area to the entrance, and attaches to it a requirement for colour contrast and distinctive patterns where the ground changes level. That requirement mainly helps people with low vision. One more fact you did not have when you approved the term: the Ontario code, which is where the term's own phrase comes from, uses it for "floors or walks", which suggests outdoor walks are included.

- **A. Yes. Widen the note to include outdoor routes.** *What it means:* the checklist's two uses are filed under your term.
- **B. Yes for the route, and record the contrast requirement separately as a provision for blind and low-vision people on that route.** *What it means:* this is the same as A, and the low-vision provision is not hidden inside a wheelchair term, which keeps your separation of the two.
- **C. No. Keep "through a building" as written.** *What it means:* the checklist's uses wait, with the "accessible route" question you already have.

**Assistant's recommendation (not a ruling): B.** It follows the source the term comes from, and it keeps the provision for people with low vision visible as their own.

**To answer:** "OD-52: A", "B" or "C".

---

## 7. When the project's own tools refuse something, may an assistant enter it by hand?

**The situation.** You suggested that when the project's tools cannot record something from a document, the problem should be logged so work is not held up and nothing is lost, "alongside having an agent fix it by hand". Every record in the book goes through checks before it is written. Those checks stop invented quotes, mistyped numbers and wrong attributions. The project's rules forbid writing records around those checks.

- **A. "By hand" means the assistant writes down what it meant to record, why the tool refused, and the fix it proposes, in the problem log. Once the tool is fixed, the entry is recorded through the normal checks.** *What it means:* nothing is lost, no work is held up, and every record in the book has still passed the checks. The content appears in the book a little later.
- **B. The assistant writes the record straight into the book's data, flagged, with the log entry beside it.** *What it means:* the content is usable at once, but it has skipped the checks that guard against invented or mistyped values. You would need to set limits on when this is allowed.

**Assistant's recommendation (not a ruling): A.** It gives you everything you asked for (nothing lost, nothing held up) without letting an unchecked value into the book. The work for A is already planned.

**To answer:** "OD-54: A" or "OD-54: B, within these limits: …".

---

_The nine decisions the assistant settled, for your information. Each was confirmed, with corrections, by the independent check. Any of them can be reversed with a line such as "OD-43: no, …":_
- **OD-40:** a figure the project calculates from two source figures shows those sources' own words, never a sentence of ours. A figure a source states in words is recorded as that source's own figure, not as a calculation.
- **OD-41:** a ramp slope written "1:12" is labelled rise over horizontal run in place. Your earlier answer on tidying stored figures already listed this exact case.
- **OD-42:** a figure moved between metric units (centimetres to millimetres) is shown exactly. Rounding to the nearest 5 mm or quarter inch, never on the unsafe side, stays for conversions between inches or feet and metric units.
- **OD-43:** the book says the evidence "agrees" only when controlled research and lived-experience evidence give the same value or range, resting on at least two independent sources. (See the first of the four things above.)
- **OD-45:** a search that a website blocked is recorded as not yet done and is owed again. It is never recorded as "nothing found".
- **OD-49:** the type of building, whether the work is new or existing, and indoor or outdoor are each recorded on the figure and shown as separate cases of one value. Building types are named from the documents' own words, not invented. Your three building levels stand. (See the third of the four things above.)
- **OD-50:** any document the project admits, not only a code, may add a new measurement for the book to ask about. You still read each addition.
- **OD-53:** a research pass may mark terms it meets as "not a measurement" (a thing such as a hearing loop, a word for a group or an activity, or a method), with a reason each, and never a measurement itself. The catalogue-wide pass reviews them. (See the fourth of the four things above.)
- **OD-55:** this only arises if OD-41 is reversed. A replaced record is then kept but retired, never counted twice.

186 scripts/audit/supersession_backpointer_audit.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""scripts/audit/supersession_backpointer_audit.py — currency lives at the superseded text.

WHY THIS EXISTS (RC3, DR-2026-09-26-recurring-defect-shapes-remediation.md section 4).
Binding text lives in more than five stores (DRs, the append-only ledger, the YAML
register, the `decisions` table, CLAUDE.md, the research contract and its SessionStart
copy, code comments, `sessions/*.md`), and a ruling superseding one of them was sometimes
left with no local mark: a reader who reaches the superseded sentence by grep meets it
with nothing saying it no longer holds. The fix is not a currency INDEX — that would be
the next store rule 5 forbids — it is a pointer at the text itself, anchored on quotes
that occur exactly once at both ends, checked with plain file I/O so `.ignore` cannot
hide the target (owner rulings live overwhelmingly in `sessions/`, which `.ignore` hides
from ripgrep and the Grep tool).

THE GRAMMAR, read from the ledger and from any DR using the same trailer:

    SUPERSEDES: <target path> :: "<verbatim quote from the target>"
      BY: references/project-standards.md :: "<verbatim quote from the superseding ruling>"

NORMALISATION (so a quote survives comment wrapping, YAML folding and Markdown
blockquotes): for each line, strip leading whitespace and one leading run of `#`, `>`,
`//` or `--`, join the lines with spaces, and collapse whitespace. Both quotes must
occur EXACTLY ONCE in their own file under this normalisation.

FAILS when: the target quote occurs 0 times (edited in place, which the append-not-edit
practice forbids) or more than once (ambiguous); the BY quote does not occur exactly
once in the ledger; or no line in the target quote's own paragraph, or in the paragraph
or blockquote immediately after it, both names SUPERSEDED or AMENDED and carries the BY
quote verbatim. `BY` is always required — `DATE:` lines in the ledger are not unique
(the most repeated closes thirteen entries), so a marker cannot be anchored on one.

EXAMINED counts `SUPERSEDES:` lines. Today there may be none in a fresh clone before the
first seed lands — that is NOTHING-IN-SCOPE, not a failure (CLAUDE.md section 5a): a
check with no subject must say so, not pass by finding nothing to check.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
sys.path.insert(0, str(REPO_ROOT / "scripts"))
import dbcore                                                        # noqa: E402

LEDGER = REPO_ROOT / "references" / "project-standards.md"
DR_DIR = REPO_ROOT / "decisions"

# The grammar and normalisation are ONE home, scripts/dbcore.py (rule 5): this script and
# scripts/db.py's dispose-adversarial-finding (OWNER-RULED) both anchor on the same
# quotes and must count them the same way, or a ref that passes one refuses the other.
_SUPERSEDES_RE = dbcore.LEDGER_SUPERSEDES_RE
_MARKER_WORD = re.compile(r'\b(SUPERSEDED|AMENDED)\b')


def _paragraphs(text: str):
    """[(start_line, end_line, normalised_joined_text)], blank-normalised-line delimited.

    A blockquote's blank line is often `>` alone, which normalises to "" here too, so a
    blockquote paragraph is delimited the same way as a plain-prose one.
    """
    lines = text.split("\n")
    normed = [dbcore.strip_ledger_line_marker(l) for l in lines]
    paras, cur_start, cur = [], None, []
    for i, n in enumerate(normed):
        if n:
            cur_start = i if cur_start is None else cur_start
            cur.append(n)
        elif cur:
            paras.append((cur_start, i - 1, " ".join(cur)))
            cur_start, cur = None, []
    if cur:
        paras.append((cur_start, len(lines) - 1, " ".join(cur)))
    return paras, lines


def _find_paragraph(paras, quote_norm: str):
    for idx, (start, end, joined) in enumerate(paras):
        if quote_norm in joined:
            return idx
    return None

def _paragraph_has_marker(lines, start: int, end: int, by_quote: str) -> bool:
    raw = "\n".join(lines[start:end + 1])
    # The BY quote is checked under the SAME normalisation as everywhere else in this
    # script, via dbcore.count_ledger_quote, not as a raw substring: a marker paragraph
    # that wraps the quote across two comment lines (a leading `#`/`>` on the wrapped
    # line) would otherwise never match, and a correctly-authored marker would FAIL.
    return bool(_MARKER_WORD.search(raw)) and dbcore.count_ledger_quote(raw, by_quote) > 0


def _parse_supersedes(text: str):
    """[(target_path, target_quote, by_path, by_quote), ...] from one file's raw text."""
    return [(m.group(1), m.group(2), m.group(3), m.group(4))
            for m in _SUPERSEDES_RE.finditer(text)]


def main() -> int:
    sources = []
    if LEDGER.exists():
        sources.append(LEDGER)
    if DR_DIR.exists():
        sources.extend(sorted(DR_DIR.glob("*.md")))

    entries, text_cache = [], {}
    for src in sources:
        text = src.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        text_cache[src] = text
        for target_path, target_quote, by_path, by_quote in _parse_supersedes(text):
            entries.append((src, target_path, target_quote, by_path, by_quote))

    examined = len(entries)
    print(f"SUPERSEDES lines found (ledger + decisions/*.md): {examined}")
    if examined == 0:
        print("VERDICT: PASS — NOTHING-IN-SCOPE (no SUPERSEDES line exists yet; "
              "correct until the first seed lands, per DR-2026-09-26 section 8).")
        print("EXAMINED: 0")
        return 0

    if not LEDGER.exists():
        print(f"[ERROR] no ledger at {LEDGER.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)}, but SUPERSEDES "
              f"lines were found. Cannot verify BY quotes.")
        print(f"EXAMINED: {examined}")
        return 2
    ledger_prose = dbcore.strip_supersedes_citations(text_cache[LEDGER])

    findings = []
    target_cache = {}  # target_rel -> (text, paragraphs, lines); several entries can share one target
    for src, target_rel, target_quote, by_path, by_quote in entries:
        where = f"{src.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)} (SUPERSEDES {target_rel!r})"
        if target_rel not in target_cache:
            target_file = REPO_ROOT / target_rel
            if not target_file.exists():
                target_cache[target_rel] = None
            else:
                text = target_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
                target_cache[target_rel] = (text, *_paragraphs(text))
        cached = target_cache[target_rel]
        if cached is None:
            findings.append(f"{where}: target file does not exist.")
            continue
        target_text, paras, lines = cached
        n_target = dbcore.count_ledger_quote(target_text, target_quote)
        if n_target != 1:
            findings.append(
                f"{where}: target quote occurs {n_target} time(s) in {target_rel} "
                f"(must be exactly 1) — {'edited in place' if n_target == 0 else 'ambiguous'}.")
            continue

        if by_path != "references/project-standards.md":
            findings.append(f"{where}: BY names {by_path!r}, not the ledger — only the "
                            f"ledger is a superseding-ruling home this audit verifies.")
            continue
        n_by = dbcore.count_ledger_quote(ledger_prose, by_quote)
        if n_by != 1:
            findings.append(
                f"{where}: BY quote occurs {n_by} time(s) in the ledger's substantive "
                f"prose, excluding SUPERSEDES citation lines (must be exactly 1).")
            continue

        quote_norm = dbcore.normalise_quote_text(target_quote)
        pidx = _find_paragraph(paras, quote_norm)
        if pidx is None:
            findings.append(f"{where}: could not locate the target quote's own paragraph "
                            f"in {target_rel} (internal inconsistency — the quote counted "
                            f"once but no paragraph contains it normalised).")
            continue
        candidates = [paras[pidx]] + ([paras[pidx + 1]] if pidx + 1 < len(paras) else [])
        marked = any(_paragraph_has_marker(lines, s, e, by_quote) for s, e, _ in candidates)
        if not marked:
            findings.append(
                f"{where}: no SUPERSEDED/AMENDED line carrying the BY quote verbatim sits "
                f"in the target quote's paragraph or the one immediately after it in "
                f"{target_rel}.")

    print(f"EXAMINED: {examined}")
    if findings:
        print("VERDICT: FAIL")
        for f in findings:
            print("  * " + f)
        return 1
    print("VERDICT: PASS")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

## 2. Preconditions

**Evidence command** (read-only):

## 4. The change

Order of preference, from CLAUDE.md §8. Nothing in `scripts/` is added: the scoring is a measurement, run once, and its script lives with its report.

# Open items: what is still open in the remediation plan, and how each is to be resolved

_Written 2026-11-12 (UTC) by an Opus-class planner on the owner's instructions "resolve all open items" and "plan how to resolve all open items first". **This is a plan; it resolves nothing except the fold of the owner's fifth set of answers (step 1, section 1).** Changed: plan documents in this folder, and the generated `REMEDIATION-PLAN.md`; the ledger was not edited (its fifth-set entry was appended by the coordinating session before this pass); no script, schema, governance file, skill, database row or git state. `sha256sum data/guidebook.db` before and after: `c9ecb8461baf2d36ba73215d991f4b46ab97b25458b6b2e3b471e9b401ab7c4d`. Canadian English. Every count is a command; where a figure is printed beside one, re-run the command and trust its output, not the figure (CLAUDE.md rule 7a)._

## 0. Verdict

**The plan is not complete as to open items, and not complete as to owner decisions.** This paragraph said, after the fifth set (2026-11-12), that no register decision a task waits on was CLOSED; that stopped being true when OD-40 to OD-46 were registered on 2026-11-13. Which register decisions hold a task now is the generator's `blocking [...]` list (a CLOSED gate that a task's "Owner decisions" bullet reads), and D-27 of `REMEDIATION-WORKPLAN.md` §10, piped to `grep CLOSED`, prints the same set with each gate's reason (it agreed with the generator on 2026-11-13); `missing deps []` and the absence of a `CYCLE` line say the dependency graph is whole. Re-run; never copy the lists here:

```
python3 -I scratchpad/session_2026-11-12-pipeline-bidirectional-audit/build_batches.py | head -2
# line 1: open tasks, batches, missing deps (must be []), the longest chain, and the tasks read as merged
# line 2: decisions, blocking [the CLOSED decisions a task waits on], standing, open, unregistered
```

What is still open is listed in section 2, one row per item, each classed:

- **A** resolvable now by a plan-document, ledger (append) or generator edit;
- **B** needs a new task (tooling or research, apart, rule 10);
- **C** needs the owner;
- **D** resolvable only at execution time (a pilot, a run, a probe);
- **E** not resolvable now; accepted as a standing limit or declined, with the reason.
- **R** resolved since this plan was written (kept for the record; not counted).

Counts by class, and how many need the owner (re-run; the table is the only home of the classes):

```
F=workplan/2026-11-12-bidirectional-pipeline/OPEN-ITEMS-PLAN.md
grep -E '^\| OI-[0-9]+ \|' "$F" | grep -o -E ' \| [A-E] \| [^|]*\|$' | cut -c4 | sort | uniq -c      # per class (inventory rows only: the class is the second-last cell)
grep -E '^\| OI-[0-9]+ \|' "$F" | grep -o -E ' \| [A-E] \| [^|]*\|$' | wc -l                        # all open items
grep -E '^\| OI-[0-9]+ \|' "$F" | grep -E ' \| C \| [^|]*\|$' | cut -d'|' -f2                       # the ones that need the owner
# at writing (after the OI-13 fold): A 3, B 3, C 12, D 16, E 15; 49 open. A resolved row keeps its id with class R and is not counted (OI-13).
```

**The three findings that matter most**, in the owner's order of criteria (integrity first):

1. **`main` holds a stale copy of this workplan, and every task file would start from it** (OI-01, OI-02). PR #218 merged an earlier version; the three plan commits since, the three design files and the fifth-set ledger entry are not on `main` (`git log --oneline origin/main..origin/ccr-408aaa9b-z3e4s0`). Every task file sets `$BASE` by testing only whether `origin/main` *has* `REMEDIATION-WORKPLAN.md`, so it now picks `origin/main`, and T-018, T-026, T-055 and T-102 would stop on a missing design file, or worse, run on stale text. Nothing can start until the plan is merged.
2. **The prior workplan's agreement rules are carried by no task, yet T-110 writes the first live determinations** (OI-09). `workplan/2026-10-23-pipeline-resolution-workplan.md` is "DRAFT, NOT EXECUTED"; this plan imports its T-1a, T-2 and T-3 (as T-016, T-017, T-019) and replaces T-5 (by T-037), but its T-4 (the owner's rulings OR-4, OR-5 and OR-6: anchoring, Co-1 setting a value, unsatisfiable anchors recorded `divergent`), T-1b and T-8, and its data PRs, have no task here and no recorded decline. A first determination computed without the ruled agreement rules would misstate what the evidence supports. ## Delegated resolution 2026-11-12 — OD-24 how coarse a parameter is, and its quantity kinds

A resolution by an Opus-class model under the owner's delegation of 2026-11-12, judged against the owner's three criteria; **not the owner's words**; standing until the owner reverses it. Reasoning and evidence: `workplan/2026-11-12-bidirectional-pipeline/DELEGATED-RESOLUTIONS.md` (section OD-24).

OD-24: flat and coarse; kinds = length, gradient (ratio, percentage or degrees as notations), force, time, luminous reflectance and its contrast (LRV), colour temperature, held as rows and extended by data with a warrant; element required: no

**The resolution.** A parameter is one measured quantity, with every clause variation a typed condition and families reached by typed term pointers; two cases are two parameters only when they cannot be placed on one scale or their accessibility directions differ. Clause-level extractions are kept and reached by pointer. Each parameter states its quantity kind from a registry of kinds held as rows (seeded from what the live parameters need, not from a list typed in code) and extended by data with a warrant. A parameter need not belong to an element; elements reach parameters by term pointers, many to many.

**What decided it.** The owner's statement of 2026-11-12 (second) that too fine a grain loses the commonality needed to "unify then specify". Criterion 1: one determination per quantity, no parent and child values to keep in step. Criterion 2: one value with its conditions. Criterion 3: group differences ride on lenses, and opposite directions split. Requiring an element would recreate the container the owner deleted.

**Reversal condition.** A parameter whose cases share a scale and direction but cannot be determined together without losing a group's difference, or a kind that cannot be added without a schema change.

CONDITION: any session defining, splitting, merging or typing a parameter, or adding a quantity kind.
ACTION: (1) Keep parameters flat and coarse; apply the split test. (2) Carry variations as typed conditions. (3) State a kind from the kinds registry; add a kind by data with a warrant. (4) Require no element.
